transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-07
Start: 15:30 UTC
Duration: ~57 minutes
Attendees: Lina Park, Marcus Reed, Priya Singh (Redwood) — Jared Mills, Sofia Alvarez, Kurt Yamada, Amira Khan (HaloHealth)
Recording: yes

Summary:
Quick technical deep dive on session-store spill patterns we're seeing, prefetch heuristics, and how eviction/paging is interacting with long-context workloads. Agreed to exchange logs and run a controlled burst test.

Topics covered:
- eviction/spill mechanics and how runtime chooses keys to evict
- prefix reuse patterns causing hot-spotting
- prefetch thresholds and memory headroom tuning
- impact of quantized kernels on KV footprint and latency
- VPC/on-prem constraints for heap profiling and secure log sharing

Quick links referenced: 
- slide deck: https://redwood.app/decks/session-prefetch.pdf
- sample telemetry dashboard: https://redwood.app/dashboards/prefetch-demo

Action items (recap): see metadata above.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Lina Park: alright, um, thanks everyone for joining, we'll, we'll kick off. I'm Lina from Redwood, account lead for HaloHealth. Marcus and Priya are with me from the runtime team.
[00:18] Kurt Yamada: hey thanks, yeah appreciate you fitting this in, we've been seeing a couple strange spill events during our morning peak, wanted to do a deeper dive.
[00:28] Marcus Reed: cool, Marcus here. quick ask before we jump, can you confirm the cluster topology and whether you're running on-prem or VPC? that will change how we approach profilers and heap dumps.
[00:38] Sofia Alvarez: sure, we're a hybrid — main workload is in our us-east-1 VPC but we have a couple on-prem boxes for regulated customers. both run the same runtime image.
[00:48] Marcus Reed: perfect, thanks. that means we'll avoid requiring root on the on-prem boxes, we'll ask for logs and flamegraphs instead.
[00:56] Amira Khan: quick note — the on-prem nodes have FIPS-enabled KMS, hope that's not an issue.
[01:06] Priya Singh: not a problem, we have KMS/HSM integration docs — will share.
[01:12] Jared Mills: to set context: our top-level problem is long sessions, multi-turn clinical notes ingestion, tokens per session often 12k to 30k, and during bursts we see latency spikes and then a couple servers start spilling from the session-store to disk.
[01:28] Marcus Reed: ok that's helpful. so when you say 'spilling' do you mean your tokenstore writes to disk or the runtime's KV layer is evicting entries and page-in/out churn?
[01:38] Jared Mills: the logs say 'spill started' and we see read I/O increase, also increased CPU. we get transient 600–1200ms per-token tail latency for a minute or two.
[01:50] Marcus Reed: got it. two possible levers: increase in-memory headroom via config, or tune prefetching so the hot prefixes are kept resident. the tricky bit is prefix reuse — if many sessions reuse the same prompt prefix, we get hotspotting, which evicts other prefixes.
[02:06] Kurt Yamada: can you expand on 'prefix reuse' and why it causes eviction?
[02:12] Marcus Reed: yeah, so our session-store uses a sharded KV with LRU-ish segments per shard. when a prefix is very hot, it pins a lot of KV memory on that shard. other prefixes on that same shard get aged out because eviction is shard-local. if your workload routes similar customers to same shard, the shard gets saturated.
[02:28] Sofia Alvarez: hmm — are shards sticky per model or per instance? how do we know routing distribution?
[02:35] Priya Singh: routing is deterministic based on prefix hash at the moment; it's per-instance. we can share a map of prefix→shard for a sample timeframe. that helps spot hotspots.
[02:46] Jared Mills: we do have a small set of templates clinicians use, so that makes sense.
[02:50] Marcus Reed: right — with templates, prefix reuse is common. one quick mitigation is to enable prefix replication for top-N prefixes so those keys are stored across multiple shards to reduce hotspotting. downside: memory cost increases.
[03:03] Kurt Yamada: what's the memory delta for top-N replication? ballpark.
[03:08] Marcus Reed: depends on average KV entry size; with your median entry ~2KB we estimate 8–12% additional memory for top-100 prefixes. we'll give a computed projection once we see your distributions.
[03:20] Amira Khan: ok and the disk spill — is that inevitable when heap runs low? any way to avoid the I/O penalty?
[03:27] Marcus Reed: couple options: 1) raise in-memory cache limit (if you have headroom), 2) tune prefetch so we pre-warm likely next-prefixes during burst, and 3) adjust eviction policy to prefer long-lived session tokens. Prefetch trades CPU and memory for lower I/O.
[03:43] Lina Park: also quantization can affect KV size — are you running int8/4 quant kernels?
[03:48] Jared Mills: yes, we switched to 4-bit quant for cost — not sure effect on cache size.
[03:55] Marcus Reed: quant affects model weight memory; KV entries are token embeddings and serialized decoder state. quantizing weights doesn't directly reduce KV size, but changing batch strategy and KV compression can. we have a compact serialization toggle that trims 12–18% off KV on average, can enable that safely.
[04:13] Priya Singh: note: compact serialization increases CPU around 5% on encode/decode paths, tradeoff to consider.
[04:21] Sofia Alvarez: what about prefetch heuristics — can you describe current default?
[04:26] Marcus Reed: default uses a simple next-token predictor based on recent prefix transitions, we prefetch N=3 prefixes ahead if memory headroom > threshold. For long-context, that prediction breaks down. We had customers set dynamic N based on session length — increase prefetch for sessions with high temporal locality.
[04:44] Jared Mills: temporal locality meaning the session tends to follow same flow? yes, our clinical workflows are pretty linear.
[04:50] Marcus Reed: then raising prefetch N for those session IDs could help. We can add a session tag rule: if session length > 10k tokens and pattern entropy < X, set N=5.
[05:02] Kurt Yamada: pattern entropy? how do we measure that cheaply?
[05:06] Marcus Reed: approximate with n-gram diversity over last K prefixes; we have a lightweight estimator in the telemetry agent. low cost.
[05:14] Amira Khan: can we test prefetch without changing production? shadow mode?
[05:18] Priya Singh: yes, we suggest running a shadow prefetch experiment: run predictions and simulate prefetch cache hits in a sidecar, no writes, observe potential hit-rate uplift. Redwood can run that against an S3 trace.
[05:30] Lina Park: let's pause and align on what we need from HaloHealth ops: eviction logs, prefix hashes for a 24h window, sample session traces for the worst hour, and permission to run a shadow prefetch test on a staging cluster.
[05:45] Sofia Alvarez: can do. we'll need instructions on exact log format.
[05:49] Marcus Reed: we'll share a small script to extract the logs and a JSON schema; if FIPS prevents direct S3 links from on-prem, we can accept encrypted tar over a secure channel.
[05:59] Jared Mills: good. question — are there recommended GC tweaks or runtime flags to avoid paging? we've tuned Linux OOM killer already.
[06:08] Marcus Reed: yes, kernel GC aside, our runtime exposes a memory-eviction-watermark and soft-limit. raising soft-limit delays eviction but increases risk of OOM if an unbounded batch spikes. For controlled bursts, raising soft-limit by 10–15% during peak windows is safe if you have headroom.
[06:24] Kurt Yamada: any risks to latency if we increase soft-limit?
[06:28] Marcus Reed: the risk is increased GC pause and higher tail CPU; we recommend a staggered ramp and monitoring.
[06:34] Sofia Alvarez: about measurements — what dashboards should we look at to correlate evictions to tail latencies?
[06:40] Priya Singh: check eviction count per shard, disk read/write IOPS, per-token tail p99 latency, and prefix hit-rate. We'll share a Grafana template.
[06:50] Lina Park: can you show us a quick example of a problematic trace? Marcus, do you have one on your side?
[06:55] Marcus Reed: yeah, I pulled a 12-min window from a similar customer. share screen? let me narrate — you'll see around t+180s a burst of 10k concurrent tokens, eviction spikes, then disk reads.
[07:10] [screen-share noises - transcript note: visual data, described verbally]
[07:18] Marcus Reed: here — the prefetched keys are almost all on shard 3; you can see the reuse curve. then evictions start for shard 7 because of cross-shard imbalance, causing page-in thrash as sessions try to access evicted prefixes.
[07:32] Sofia Alvarez: that cross-shard imbalance — why would shard 3 be so hot? hash function?
[07:36] Marcus Reed: likely because your template prefixes hash-collide to same shard. Two fixes: change hash modulus (requires draining) or enable lightweight replication for top prefixes to spread reads. Replication is lower-impact operationally.
[07:50] Jared Mills: draining is painful; so replication sounds better. What's the replication window consistency model?
[07:55] Priya Singh: eventual consistency with latest-write wins for TTL-based entries; it's tuned for reads. We use async replication so writes don't add huge latency.
[08:04] Kurt Yamada: latency overhead for reads when replicated?
[08:08] Marcus Reed: negligible for reads; minor increase on write due to replication queue, usually <2ms.
[08:14] Amira Khan: earlier Marcus mentioned compact serialization; can that be toggled per-model?
[08:19] Marcus Reed: yes, per-model toggle — ideal to trial on a low-traffic model first.
[08:25] Lina Park: let's talk about prefetched-key eviction heuristics — are we evicting based purely on recency or cost-aware?
[08:31] Marcus Reed: current default is recency-weighted LRU. we also support a cost-aware heuristic that considers the estimated recompute cost of a key (inference compute + disk I/O). For your workloads where recompute cost is high, cost-aware helps.
[08:43] Sofia Alvarez: how do you estimate recompute cost? is it model-dependent?
[08:47] Marcus Reed: yes, model+sequence-length dependent. we use a small predictor trained on tokenization and kernel latency profiles. we'll send the predictor spec.
[08:56] Jared Mills: if we switch to cost-aware, do we need to retrain anything?
[09:00] Marcus Reed: no retraining on your side — it's a config flip but we recommend validating in shadow mode first.
[09:06] Priya Singh: note: cost-aware tends to keep slightly larger set resident so expect memory uptick ~5%.
[09:13] Kurt Yamada: let's zoom out to quantization — we saw CPU spikes earlier; could quant kernels be causing increased per-token CPU during page-in?
[09:21] Marcus Reed: when weights are quantized, some kernels use slower fallback paths for certain sequence lengths; combined with de-serialization cost of KV, you could see CPU increase. Also if your runtime is decompressing KV entries with compact serialization, that is CPU-heavy.
[09:34] Amira Khan: so tradeoffs all over. is there a recommended first-pass config change that is low-risk?
[09:41] Marcus Reed: yes: enable compact serialization for model X in staging, run shadow prefetch with N=4 for tagged sessions, and set soft-limit +10% during the controlled burst. Those are reversible quickly.
[09:55] Lina Park: ok, we'll propose that as the test plan.
[09:58] Sofia Alvarez: security question — if you need access to logs from our VPC, what's the least-privilege approach?
[10:03] Priya Singh: best is to drop logs into a customer-owned S3 bucket with a limited IAM role we assume (STS) for 1 hour. For on-prem, encrypted tar via secure transfer. We'll provide an automation script.
[10:15] Kurt Yamada: SOC2 and data retention compliance: how long do Redwood retention logs keep session artifacts? we need to ensure PHI isn't kept longer.
[10:24] Lina Park: Redwood can configure tenant-level retention; default is 30 days for full transcript artifacts, but for customers with PHI we can do 7 days or disable. We'll attach our SOC2 summary in the follow-up.
[10:36] Jared Mills: great. a gotcha: some of our sessions start in on-prem and later route to VPC — does that break prefix routing and cause prefix-to-shard mismatch?
[10:45] Marcus Reed: it can if the instance hash space differs; we recommend sticky routing or a centralized hash ring. We'll share a migration checklist to avoid mismatches.
[10:55] Amira Khan: let's talk about measuring success — what does a successful pilot look like?
[11:00] Marcus Reed: measurable goals: reduce spill events by 80% in peak windows, reduce p99 token latency from ~1s to <300ms, and keep additional memory cost <15%.
[11:10] Sofia Alvarez: sounds good.
[11:12] Marcus Reed: last technical note — there is a subtle bug we found in older runtime builds where prefix eviction timestamps were off-by-one leading to premature evictions under heavy GC. which version are you running?
[11:22] Jared Mills: 2.3.1.
[11:24] Marcus Reed: ok, that build is impacted; patch 2.3.4 has the fix. we recommend patching staging first.
[11:31] Lina Park: we'll include upgrade steps in the notes.
[11:34] [long pause / background typing sounds]
[11:43] Marcus Reed: quick run-through of the planned experiment: 1) collect 24h logs + top prefixes, 2) run shadow prefetch on a trace, 3) enable compact serialization in staging for model X, 4) enable replication for top-100 prefixes, 5) run controlled burst with soft-limit+10% ramp.
[12:03] Jared Mills: agreed. estimated effort on our side?
[12:06] Priya Singh: about 2–3 engineer-days to gather artifacts and coordinate the burst window.
[12:12] Sofia Alvarez: we can commit that.
[12:14] Marcus Reed: one more pointer — if you prefer not to use replication, an alternate is to change shard hashing to siphash2 to spread templates more evenly, but that requires draining nodes which is heavy.
[12:28] Kurt Yamada: ok replication sounds better.
[12:30] Lina Park: let's open it up for any final questions.
[12:33] Amira Khan: small question — buffer sizes for the disk writer, can you tune that?
[12:37] Marcus Reed: yes adjustable, default is 4MB, increasing can batch writes and reduce IOPS but increases latency on flush. we can propose values for your I/O profile.
[12:47] Jared Mills: how will we verify the patch 2.3.4 reduces premature evictions? any smoke test?
[12:52] Marcus Reed: yes, we'll provide a smoke test that simulates the eviction pattern and checks timestamps; we can run it in staging quickly.
[13:00] [audio overlap, someone mutes/unmutes]
[13:06] Kurt Yamada: thanks — action items recap?
[13:09] Lina Park: Marcus, Priya — share scripts, dashboard template, and prefetch simulation instructions. HaloHealth — share logs and schedule burst test. We'll aim for next sync after the shadow run.
[13:20] Jared Mills: perfect, thanks everyone.
[13:24] Lina Park: end note: we'll attach SOC2 blurbs and the KMS integration doc in the follow-up email. Thanks, bye.
[56:30] [meeting ended]
